SPM261.02 Soccer League Rulebook 
 SPM261.02 Soccer League — Rulebook
 Fall 2026 · every rule, every formula, every point your grade is built from
 Overview
 You are not a player — you are the owner and general manager of a professional soccer club.
 Every decision a real front office makes — who to draft, how to line up, what to charge for tickets, which sponsor
 to sign, which trades to make, and how far you push for a championship — is yours to make, in writing, every round.
 Your grade is not just whether you win. It is whether you can run a sports business and explain why you made the calls
 you made.
 1. The Season Scorecard — Your Grade
 100 points across four components. Ranking and Revenue are scored
 relative to the rest of the league — 1st place earns full points, and every place below the one
 above it costs a flat 1 point, not a fraction of the whole component spread evenly down to zero.
 Finishing last still costs you real points relative to your classmates, but it does not wipe out the entire
 component the way an even 1st-to-0 spread would.
 Component Points Question it answers How it's scored 
 Standings Rank 40 Did your team win? 1st = 40, −1 pt per place down (last of 20 = 21) 
 Playoff Qualification 5 Did you make the playoffs? Flat: full 5 pts for finishing in the top 6, 0 otherwise — not tiered, since finishing 1st vs. 6th is already rewarded by Ranking 
 Business Revenue 35 Did you run it as a business? 1st = 35, −1 pt per place down (last of 20 = 16) — ticket + sponsorship + national TV + local TV revenue 
 Decision Rationale 20 Could you explain your calls? Average grade on the written explanation you submit with your Weekly Lineup, as a % of 20 
 A well-reasoned decision that loses to bad luck scores exactly as well, on Rationale, as one
 that wins. A last-place team still earns 21 of 40 Ranking points and
 16 of 35 Revenue points just for being in the league, and a last-place team
 that runs a genuinely profitable franchise can still score well on Revenue. There is more than one way to earn
 a strong grade here.
 Worked Example
 A team that wins the league (40/40 — full ranking points), qualifies for the playoffs by finishing top
 6 (5/5), finishes 3rd in league revenue out of 20 teams (33 pts), and
 averages a strong rationale score (17.5 of 20) lands at
 40 + 5 + 33 + 17.5 = 95.5 out of 100.
 2. Decision Rationale Rubric
 Every round, your written rationale is scored against 4 criteria, 4 points each (16 possible; Business/Financial
 Reasoning is excluded on a plain lineup round with no trade/sponsorship attached, graded out of 12 instead). Your
 season average, as a percentage, becomes the 20-point Rationale component above.
 Criterion 1 — Minimal 2 — Developing 3 — Proficient 4 — Exemplary 
 Strategic Fit Unexplained or contradicts your own analysis Stated but the link to the opponent/roster is vague Clearly justified by a specific comparison Reflects a specific tactical read and anticipates a counter-response 
 Use of Data No reference to ratings/stats/standings Mentions a stat without connecting it to the decision Cites specific ratings or standings/financial data Integrates multiple data points into one argument 
 Business/Financial Reasoning No cap/budget/revenue consideration Acknowledges a cost without weighing it Weighs cost against benefit explicitly Frames it as a tradeoff among goals and states the priority 
 Adaptability No reference to prior results Mentions a past result without changing the call Explicitly adjusts based on a prior outcome Names the signal, the lesson, and the causal link to this round 
 Full descriptors: rubric/Decision_Rationale_Rubric.docx .
 3. League Structure
 Setting Value 
 Teams 20 (one per student — solo ownership, no co-owners) 
 Roster size 18 players per team 
 Starting budget $15,000,000 
 Salary cap $18,000,000 
 Sponsorship 6 categories, one brand each, mandatory — sponsors pay you 
 Regular season Round-robin — every team plays every other team once 
 Playoffs Top 6 teams by regular-season standings 
 4. Player Ratings
 Every player carries six ratings, 0–99 (the same convention as most sports video games):
 Rating What it measures 
 ATT Attack — finishing and creativity, the biggest input to scoring chances 
 DEF Defense — tackling, positioning, shot-stopping 
 PAC Pace — speed and recovery, a secondary contributor both ways 
 PHY Physical — strength and stamina, a secondary contributor both ways 
 OVR Overall — a quick-reference blend of the four above (NOT what the match engine uses directly) 
 Star Power Marketability — deliberately independent of skill. Drives sponsorship eligibility and ticket demand. 
 Weekly Player Condition
 ATT and DEF above are a player's fixed BASE ratings — what actually goes into a match is scaled by that
 player's CONDITION for that specific round, redrawn every round for every player. A player who was excellent last
 week can be off this week, and vice versa — last week's lineup is not automatically this week's right call.
 Condition Multiplier Odds 
 Poor 0.85x 10% 
 Below Average 0.93x 20% 
 Average 1.00x 40% 
 Good 1.07x 20% 
 Excellent 1.15x 10% 
 Condition is drawn once per player per round, from a fixed formula (your season seed + the round number + that
 player's ID) — not random in a way that can be gamed, and not knowable before the league office publishes it.
 It is published before that round's Weekly Lineup deadline , both on the live dashboard (each roster
 card shows a Condition badge per player) and as a standalone report ( engine/generate_weekly_conditions.py )
 specifically so it's real information your starting XI and formation choice should account for, not a surprise
 revealed only in the result. A bench player in Excellent form can outperform a starter having a Poor week —
 reading the weekly report before you submit is part of the job.
 Injuries
 Every player who actually STARTS a match carries a 6% chance of picking up an
 injury that round — unlike the routine week-to-week Condition roll above, an injury is a CONSEQUENCE of
 playing, not a fresh dice roll every week, and it doesn't clear on its own until it runs its course.
 What Detail 
 Chance per start 6% 
 Duration 1–3 rounds, randomly, once injured 
 Effective multiplier while injured 0.55x 
 While injured, a player's Condition badge shows "Injured" together with the round they come back
 (for example "Injured · back Round 6") — visible on the dashboard and in the weekly report exactly like ordinary form,
 before you submit. An already-injured player who gets started anyway just keeps counting down; they cannot get
 newly hurt on top of an existing injury. Bench them, or play them at a real, known cost — that decision, and
 being able to see it coming, is the point. Injured players can be treated on the Player Health Hub
 (Section 5).
 5. Player Health Hub
 From Round 3, owners can pay for treatment on the
 Player Health Hub . Every treatment applies to the next round to be played and is paid
 from your team's cash on hand (shown on the Budget Dashboard). Spending reduces cash only; it does not reduce the
 Revenue component of the Season Scorecard.
 Treatment For Effect Cost 
 Standard Rehab Injured players Returns 1 round sooner $75,000 
 Accelerated Rehab Injured players Returns 2 rounds sooner $200,000 
 Elite Specialist Clinic Injured players Fit for next round, at Average condition $375,000 
 Recovery Session Healthy players +1 condition level next round $50,000 
 Sports-Science Package Healthy players +2 condition levels next round (max Excellent) $125,000 
 Limit: 4 treatments per team per round, one per player. Condition cannot rise above
 Excellent. Requests are processed about every 30 minutes, and the weekly Player Condition report updates to show
 the effect before you submit your lineup. A request that fails a check (not enough cash, round already played,
 limit reached) is voided at no cost. Explain any treatment in that round's lineup rationale; it is scored under
 Business/Financial Reasoning.
 How to book: open the Player Health Hub , choose your team, enter your
 team PIN, pick the player and the treatment, and submit. Book before you submit that round's Weekly Lineup, then
 check the Player Condition report to confirm the treatment took effect.
 Thinking like a general manager: treatment is an investment decision. Weigh the cost against what
 the player is worth to your result this round: a star forward back two rounds early in a tight playoff race is
 worth far more than a squad player in a match you are expected to win comfortably.
 6. The Draft
 Before the season begins, every owner drafts a full roster from the shared player pool. Two hard rules apply:
 Roster size is fixed at 18 players, filling every slot your formation choices require.
 Total roster salary may never exceed the $18,000,000 salary cap — at draft time or afterward.
 Undrafted players remain Free Agents, signable later in the season.
 How the Draft Actually Runs
 A real live snake draft — 18 rounds × 20 teams — is hundreds of
 sequential picks, far more than one class period holds. So Draft Day is a reveal, not a wait :
 Before Draft Day: submit a ranked Draft Board of at least 25 players (more than
 the 18 you need, so you still have real choices left once some of your targets are gone).
 Draft order: one randomized snake order (Round 1 picks 1…20, Round 2 picks
 20…1, alternating), drawn reproducibly from the season seed — the exact order can be
 independently re-verified after the fact, same principle as every match result.
 Live in class: the league office runs the resolution engine once, in front of everyone. At your
 turn each round, you get the highest-ranked player still on YOUR board who's still available and still fits under
 your remaining cap space — instant, no live back-and-forth required.
 If your whole board runs out before your roster is full (bad luck — too many targets taken
 ahead of you): autopick takes the highest-OVR player still available and affordable — same "league office
 auto-fills" fallback used for a missed Trade Day pairing.
 7. Weekly Operations
 Every round, before the deadline, each owner submits a Weekly Lineup & Strategy form: formation, strategy,
 starting XI by name, a ticket price if home that round, and a 2–4 sentence rationale (graded — see the grading table below).
 Check that round's Player Condition report first (see Player Ratings above) — it's published before the
 deadline specifically so your starting XI and formation choice can react to who's actually in form this week, not
 just who has the highest base rating.
 If you do not submit a complete Weekly Lineup — every field, including your decision
 rationale — by the deadline (or your submission is rejected for a wrong PIN), your team is penalized for that
 round and you earn no rationale credit.
 Medical decisions: from Round 3, you can also book paid treatment for injured or out-of-form players on
 the Player Health Hub (Section 5). Book it before you submit your lineup, and explain it in your rationale.

 9. How Match Results Are Determined
 Results are not a coin flip, and not roster OVR alone — every result traces to the lineup, formation, and
 strategy you actually submitted:
 Each starter's ATT/DEF is first scaled by their Weekly Player Condition for this round (see Player Ratings above), then
 your starting XI's (condition-adjusted) ATT/DEF become one Team Attack and one Team Defense score, weighted by
 formation.
 Your Strategy choice shifts that balance further.
 The home team gets a fixed +5% Attack bonus.
 Attack vs. opposing Defense produces an expected-goals (xG) number for each side — a big mismatch caps
 out rather than producing an unrealistic blowout.
 The actual score is drawn randomly around each side's xG — the deliberate "luck" every real match has.
 A stronger team is more likely to win, never guaranteed to.
 Every match's random draw is seeded from the season's fixed seed plus that exact matchup — any result can
 be independently re-verified after the fact, and nothing is adjustable after the fact by the league office.
 10. Ticket Sales & Attendance
 As the home team, you set a ticket price tier. Attendance responds to price AND to your recent form and
 starting-XI Star Power:
 Tier Price Effect 
 Budget $15 Fills more seats, caps per-ticket revenue 
 Standard $30 Neutral default 
 Premium $50 Highest per-ticket revenue, but demand drops sharply without form/Star Power to justify it 
 There is no universally correct price — a struggling, low-Star-Power team pricing Premium will earn LESS
 than pricing Standard or Budget. Read your own team's market every home match.
 Away gate share: the away team does not set a price, but it still earns a cut of that match's
 gate — 5% to 15% of the home side's ticket revenue, scaled by the AWAY team's own recent form and
 starting-XI Star Power (a hot, star-studded traveling team draws more visiting-fan interest). A winless,
 zero-Star-Power away team earns the 5% floor; a team on a hot streak with strong starters earns up to the 15%
 ceiling. The home side still keeps the large majority of its own gate either way.
 11. Sponsorship Deals & Negotiation
 Sponsors pay you — there is no cost to sign anything, matching how real sponsorship deals
 work. Brands are grouped into 6 categories (real clubs carry exactly one jersey sponsor, one kit
 manufacturer, one official airline — not an unlimited pile of deals), and every team MUST sign
 exactly one brand per category before the draft ends — this is mandatory, not optional.
 Multiple teams may hold the same brand (Nike sponsors many real clubs at once); the "slots" number on each brand is
 a league-wide cap, not an exclusivity lock.
 On your turn (same turn-order format as the player draft, cycling through all 6 categories), target
 an open brand in whichever category you're filling. Two separate things are on the table:
 Revenue
 Take the listed Base revenue exactly (guaranteed, zero risk), or Negotiate. Negotiating lands you anywhere from
 −10% to +10% of the brand's base revenue, set by your Negotiating Leverage 
 (built from your roster's average Star Power, plus a standings bonus once the season starts): leverage 0 lands at
 −10%, leverage 50 lands exactly at base, leverage 100 lands at +10%. Negotiating is not risk-free the way
 taking Base is — a weak hand can genuinely land below base.
 The commission: whenever a negotiated deal lands away from base — in EITHER direction
 — that gap is ALSO credited as bonus revenue to whichever team's student played the sponsor rep in that
 negotiation. Land above base (good for the signing team) and the overage goes to the rep's team; talk the team
 down below base (good for the sponsor) and the savings goes to the rep's team instead. Landing exactly at base
 earns nobody a commission, since nothing was actually negotiated. Never a deduction from the signing team's own
 booked revenue either way.
 AI Sponsor Rep. Brands can also be negotiated one-on-one with the AI Sponsor Rep page. The same
 leverage rule sets how far each brand will go (a strong, data-backed pitch can add a little), the rep may walk
 away from owners who keep asking far more than it will pay, and no sponsor-rep commission is earned, since no
 student played the rep. Big brands choose contenders: Nike, Red Bull, Visa, Emirates, BMW and Samsung only
 negotiate with clubs at Negotiating Leverage 40+, and Adidas, Mastercard and Qatar Airways need 30+. With the
 AI rep, a clause request names the clause you want: one step looser than the brand's opening clause needs
 leverage 20+, two steps 50+, and strict to no clause 80+.
 Clause
 A separate ask: push for a looser clause at Modest / Bold / Very Bold intensity, gated by the same leverage
 number. Ask beyond what your leverage supports and the brand walks away on the clause specifically — that
 costs you nothing on the revenue side, and you can simply not push the clause further.

 The performance clause is not flavor text -- it is real revenue at risk, and each clause level sets its OWN

 This is checked PER DEAL, off your one final rank -- a team can clear a loose-clause deal's easy bar while

 12. TV / Broadcast Revenue
 League-Wide (National) TV Deal
 Base: $800,000 per team.
 Standings bonus: Top team at split time: +1,000,000. 2nd: +600,000. 3rd: +300,000. Bottom 3 teams: +0 (no penalty beyond missing the bonus).
 Star Power bonus: If a team's average starting-XI Star Power ranks in the league's top 3 at split time, add +500,000 (broadcasters pay for star wattage independent of the standings) -- this can stack with the standings bonus.
 Split timing: After round 3 of the 19-round regular season (20 teams, round-robin).
 Local TV Deals
 A per-team regional broadcast contract, separate from and additional to the league-wide national TV deal above -- modeled on how real clubs also carry an individual local/regional media deal that varies hugely by market size, on top of a shared national split. Assigned once, right after Draft Day (engine/generate_local_tv_deals.py -> data/local_tv_deals.json), and fixed for the whole season like a real regional broadcast contract -- not renegotiated mid-season.
 Market tiers: Every team is randomly assigned exactly one of five market tiers, split as evenly as possible across the league and drawn reproducibly from season_seed: Major Market (strict clause), Large Market (strict clause), Mid Market (standard clause), Small Market (standard clause), Micro Market (loose clause) -- higher-value markets carry a stricter clause, the same pattern Sponsorship's brand table uses. Your market tier's actual base rate is not publicly posted -- your network rep tells you the number face to face when you sit down to negotiate, the same convention Sponsorship uses for its own brand base revenue.
 Market Tier Base Clause

 Star Power modifier: If a team's average starting-XI Star Power ranks in the league's top 3 at split time, its Local TV Deal pays +15% that round -- same top-3 threshold as the national deal's star bonus, scaled off the team's own base (proportional) rather than a flat dollar add, since a Major Market base and a Micro Market base already differ so much in size.
 Payout timing: Paid out at the same midseason split point as the national TV deal (after Round 3 of the 19-round regular season) -- one TV Revenue Day covers both national and local money at once.
 Local TV revenue flows into the team's budget like any other revenue; it never raises the salary cap itself.
 Local TV Rights Negotiation
 Right after Draft Day, every team negotiates its Local TV Deal live, in class, against a rotating peer playing the network rep (engine/generate_tv_negotiation_rotation.py pairs everyone once, no repeat partners; an odd team count leaves one bye, filled by the instructor). Exactly like Sponsorship, TWO separate things are on the table -- same mechanic, same functions in engine/negotiation.py. Revenue: take the market-tier Base rate exactly (guaranteed, zero risk), or Negotiate to land anywhere from -10% to +10% of it, set by your Negotiating Leverage (built from your roster average Star Power, plus a standings bonus once the season starts). Your market tier's exact base rate is not publicly posted anywhere -- your network rep tells you the number face to face at the start of the negotiation, the same convention Sponsorship uses for its own brand base revenue. Clause: a separate ask -- push for a looser clause than your market tier's base clause, at Modest/Bold/Very Bold intensity, gated by the same leverage number against a required threshold; an unsuccessful ask can walk away (clause stays at base, no revenue impact). The commission: whenever a negotiated rate lands away from base -- in EITHER direction -- that gap is ALSO credited immediately (not at the Round 3 split) as bonus revenue to whichever team played the network rep. Above base rewards the negotiating team's win; below base (a good deal for the network) rewards the rep instead, same size commission, mirrored direction -- same either-direction logic as a sponsorship commission. Landing exactly at base earns nobody a commission. This negotiation sets the RATE and the CLAUSE only; the money itself is still paid at the Round 3 split above, with the Star Power modifier still applied on top then, and the clause is checked once at season end exactly like a sponsorship clause (see clause_enforcement above -- the same rank thresholds apply to Local TV deals). The League-Wide (National) TV Deal is not part of this exercise -- it is a shared, formula-only split with no natural second party to negotiate against.
 Clause
 Exactly like Sponsorship, a Local TV Deal's clause is a separate ask from its rate: push for a looser
 clause than your market tier's base clause, at Modest / Bold / Very Bold intensity, gated by your same
 Negotiating Leverage number. Ask beyond what your leverage supports and the deal walks away on the clause
 specifically — that costs you nothing on the revenue side, and you can simply not push the clause
 further. See "What the Clause Actually Means" in the Sponsorship Deals & Negotiation section above for
 the rank-threshold table — the
 same thresholds and the same 20% penalty apply to a Local TV Deal's clause, checked
 once at season end off your one final rank.
 13. Trades & Free Agency
 Deadline: Trades must be fully agreed to (both teams accepted) before Round 7 -- Round 6 is the last round a trade can still land. No trades take effect in Rounds 7-19 or at any point after -- this prevents last-minute roster stacking right before the playoff-qualification picture is set, the same reason real leagues carry a trade deadline.
 How many players: Every trade must send the SAME number of players back each way -- 1-for-1, 2-for-2, or 3-for-3 only, never an uneven count like 1-for-2. On top of that, a team may trade away at most 3 players total, combining every trade it makes, before the Round 6 deadline -- once a team has moved 3 players, it's done trading for the season, win or lose on those swaps.
 Voluntary: Trading is entirely optional. No team is required to make a trade, and nobody has to accept an offer just because it's sent -- if the two sides can't agree on fair value, the simplest right answer is to not trade.
 Salary cap rule: A trade is only valid if BOTH teams remain at or under salary_cap (see league_config.json) after the trade completes.
 Cash considerations: Either side may add cash (from its budget, not a salary-cap item) on top of the player swap to make up for a value gap -- paying extra cash to land a clearly better player than what you're giving up is a normal, allowed trade structure, the same way real clubs attach cash to a deal.
 Approval: A trade only takes effect once BOTH teams agree to it: the proposing team submits a Trade Proposal, and it sits pending until the receiving team accepts or declines it on the Trade Center page. Accepting applies it immediately (once it clears the roster/cap checks below); declining ends it with no changes to either roster.
 Trade Day
